summary: Describes Topology Dissemination Based on Reverse-Path Forwarding (TBRPF), a proactive link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks that provides hop-by-hop shortest-path routing. Each node computes a source tree from partial topology information, and the protocol is designed to keep overhead low. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Moving devices need to find paths to each other. Each device keeps only a part of the map and shares small updates, so it saves effort while still finding short routes.

questions: link state routing for ad hoc networks
how does tbrpf differ from ospf
subtitle: A link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks that keeps overhead low by sharing only part of each node's route tree.

tldr.problem: Classical link-state protocols such as OSPF send a lot of control traffic, which is a poor fit for mobile ad hoc networks where nodes move and the radio channel is shared.
tldr.mechanism: Each node computes a source tree with a modification of Dijkstra's algorithm, reports only part of that tree to its neighbors using periodic and differential updates, and finds neighbors with small differential HELLO messages.
tldr.outcome: The result is hop-by-hop routing along shortest paths with far less control traffic than classical link-state routing. The RFC is Experimental, and RFC 9141 updates it.

today: RFC 3684 is an Experimental specification, not an Internet standard, and it is updated by RFC 9141. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Proactive Routing With Partial Topology
sections.content:
TBRPF (Topology Dissemination Based on Reverse-Path Forwarding) is a proactive, link-state routing protocol for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). Proactive means each node keeps routes to all reachable destinations at all times, whether or not there is traffic for them. TBRPF gives hop-by-hop routing along shortest paths.

It has two modules. The neighbor discovery module finds the nodes a router can hear directly. The routing module learns the topology and computes routes. Each node builds a source tree, the shortest-path tree from itself to every reachable node, from the partial topology stored in its topology table.

The saving comes from reporting only part of that tree, called the reported subtree, to neighbors. A node reports the subtrees rooted at neighbors that might pick it as their next hop. Received updates are not forwarded as they are; they may only change what a node reports next. The RFC says TBRPF can support networks of up to a few hundred nodes, and can be combined with hierarchical routing for much larger ones.
sections.eli5: Imagine a class where every kid knows who sits next to them. Instead of everyone shouting the whole seating chart, each kid only passes on the part of the chart that their neighbors need.

sections.title: Packets and Message Types
sections.content:
TBRPF data travels in packets made of a header and a body of one or more messages. The header is at least one octet. It carries a 4-bit version (this document describes version 4), flags L and I, and two reserved bits that MUST be zero. L says a 16-bit length follows, and I says a 4-octet router ID follows. A sender sets them only when the underlying delivery service does not already supply that information.

Each message in the body starts with 4 option bits and a 4-bit TYPE. Receivers MUST process elements strictly in order, and on a malformed message they MUST stop processing the packet and discard what is left.

The three HELLO subtypes (NEIGHBOR REQUEST, REPLY and LOST) each carry an 8-bit sequence number HSEQ, a 4-bit relay priority and a 12-bit count of neighbor interface addresses. Relay priority is 0 to 15. A router in normal operation SHOULD use 7, and 0 marks a non-relay node that never forwards other nodes' packets.

The routing module adds the TOPOLOGY UPDATE messages (FULL, ADD, DELETE) and three association messages that bind extra interface addresses, host addresses and network prefixes to a router ID.
sections.eli5: Every note TBRPF sends has a little label saying what kind of note it is. Receivers read the notes in the order they come and throw out the rest of the page if one note looks broken.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery With Differential HELLOs
sections.content:
The TBRPF Neighbor Discovery protocol (TND) finds bidirectional links quickly. Unlike OSPF, whose HELLOs list every neighbor, TND sends differential HELLOs that report only changes in link status. That makes HELLOs much smaller, so they can be sent more often.

Each link is LOST, 1-WAY or 2-WAY. To avoid links that are likely to be short lived, a node must receive at least HELLO_ACQUIRE_COUNT (default 2) of the last HELLO_ACQUIRE_WINDOW (default 3) HELLOs from a neighbor interface before calling the link 1-WAY. It then lists that neighbor in NEIGHBOR REQUEST for its next NBR_HOLD_COUNT (default 3) HELLOs. The neighbor answers with NEIGHBOR REPLY and both sides call the link 2-WAY.

A link goes to LOST when NBR_HOLD_COUNT HELLOs are missed or nothing is heard within NBR_HOLD_TIME (default 3 seconds). The node announces this in NEIGHBOR LOST, so both ends agree the link is no longer bidirectional. Nodes MUST send at least one HELLO per HELLO_INTERVAL (default 1 second), and SHOULD vary the spacing slightly with a random jitter of up to 0.1 second. A link-layer failure notice, where available, lets a node declare a 2-WAY link LOST at once.
sections.eli5: Neighbors say "hi" to each other all the time. They only talk about changes, like "I can hear you now" or "I lost you", so the messages stay tiny.

sections.title: Routing: Source Tree and Reported Subtree
sections.content:
Each node runs a variant of Dijkstra's algorithm on its topology graph to get the source tree and then the routing table. Equal-cost ties are broken by router ID. Two small penalties apply: NON_REPORT_PENALTY (1.01) for links not reported by the parent, and NON_TREE_PENALTY (0.01) for links not already in the tree, which reduces tree changes. Link metrics are optional (USE_METRICS defaults to 0, meaning hop counts).

A node reports a neighbor in its reported node set only if one of its neighbors might choose it as next hop to that neighbor. It works this out from shortest paths of up to 2 hops between neighbors, using relay priority and router ID to break ties. The reported subtree is the part of the source tree rooted at those nodes, plus the node's own links.

Updates come in two forms. A periodic update carries the whole reported subtree every PER_UPDATE_INTERVAL (default 5 seconds). A differential update carries only additions and deletions every DIFF_UPDATE_INTERVAL (default 1 second). There are no ACKs or NACKs and no sequence numbers on topology updates. Instead, for each link only the report from the next hop toward its tail is believed. Topology information expires after TOP_HOLD_TIME (default 15 seconds).

A node may also report extra links for robustness, up to the full topology. If it does, IMPLICIT_DELETION MUST be 0.
sections.eli5: Each kid draws the shortest path to every classmate and shares just the part of the drawing that helps their neighbors. Every few seconds they send a small "what changed" note, and now and then the full drawing.

sections.title: Running TBRPF on a MANET
sections.content:
TBRPF packets normally travel over UDP/IP. IANA has assigned port 712 for it. Over IPv4 they go to the All Routers multicast address 224.0.0.2, and TBRPF routers MUST NOT forward packets sent there. IPv6 operation is the same, with 128-bit addresses, but router IDs stay at 32 bits. The data delivery service MUST provide a checksum.

TBRPF also describes an optional flooding mechanism for network-wide broadcast. A node retransmits a flooded packet, sent to 224.0.1.20, only if it has not seen it before, the source is in its reported node set, and the TTL is still above zero after decrementing. That is far fewer transmissions than classical flooding.

Multiple interfaces, alias addresses, network prefixes and non-MANET hosts are advertised with the association messages. HELLOs carry both link-layer and network-layer addresses, so implementations MAY learn address bindings from them instead of using ARP.
sections.eli5: TBRPF sends its notes only to the kids sitting next to you, and only a few chosen kids pass a shout-out along to the rest of the room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that wireless networks face denial-of-service, man-in-the-middle and service-theft attacks. It stresses preventing spoofing of TBRPF nodes and stopping unauthorized nodes from joining through neighbor discovery. TBRPF packets can be authenticated with the IP Authentication Header, and the Encapsulating Security Payload header can add confidentiality. The RFC also says TBRPF can be extended to use SEND mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Anyone nearby can pretend to be a classmate on a radio network, so the notes should be signed, and secret ones should be locked.

items.desc: Two or more octets of padding.

items.label: NEIGHBOR REQUEST
items.desc: HELLO subtype listing neighbors heard but not yet 2-way.

items.label: TOPOLOGY UPDATE: FULL
items.desc: All reported links with a given tail.

items.label: TOPOLOGY UPDATE: ADD
items.desc: Links added to the reported subtree.

items.label: TOPOLOGY UPDATE: DELETE
items.desc: Links removed from the reported subtree.

items.label: INTERFACE ASSOCIATION
items.desc: Interface addresses tied to a router ID.

items.label: HOST ASSOCIATION
items.desc: Host addresses tied to a router ID.

items.label: NETWORK PREFIX ASSOCIATION
items.desc: Network prefixes tied to a router ID.
